machine.shared: A development machine, at rest for this study: every round ran under the lock of the measurements; the two agents of the machine, a logcenter and three gates of an application stayed up, idle

build.tls: OpenSSL 3.6.5 (bundled, static: linux-ext-libs 1.31 in 7.32.0, 1.28 in 7.31.1); mbedTLS not built on this machine

method.ab: Written on 2026-11-22, before the tag. 7.32.0 is the C code of 318204992, its version commit (the release commit after it changes no .c file), measured against 7.31.1, the last release with a study; the 28 lite releases between them (7.31.2 to 7.31.29) were never studied. Between the two sides: 232 commits, 19,323 lines added and 1,166 removed in .c and .h (7,863 and 1,059 outside the tests and the benchmarks). Both sides are git worktrees (yunetas-perf-7.31.1 at 3c53c9075 and yunetas-perf-head) built by `yunetas init --sdk-only` and `make install` of the kernel libraries and modules into their own outputs/, the benchmarks and the three ctest binaries from their root build/, the yunos by make. Each side has the linux-ext-libs of its release: 1.28 for 7.31.1, 1.31 for 7.32.0 (jansson 2.15.1-yuneta.2; mbedTLS 4.3.0 and nginx 1.31.9 are not in these binaries). The binaries pinned to one CPU (taskset -c 6) and run in rotation, the order turned each round, a sync and a 3 s pause (1 s for the three ctest binaries) before each run: 10 rounds. Mean +- standard deviation (median), t = the change over its standard error; |t| < 3 is noise. The eight figures outside their noise were measured again, 10 more rounds of their six benchmarks (perf_timeranger2, perf_tr_treedb, perf_auth_bff, perf_tcp_test4, perf_tcps_test4, perf_mqtt), and their reasons give both runs and the 20 rounds together. The losses that held were located by tag: 7.31.24, 7.31.25 and 7.31.29 built in scratch worktrees (each with linux-ext-libs 1.31, as their releases had) and run in one rotation with both sides, 8 rounds; then 7.31.1 with the linux-ext-libs of 7.32.0, and five commits of 7.32.0 (d5feb36c8, 17fc90a4a, 78b98acb5, 60aac358a, 7de398cfb), in one more rotation of 8 rounds. The BFF figure and the event loop echoes are means of the samples of a run, the first left out (and the last, for the echoes). The treedb figures (perf_tr_treedb, perf_tr_treedb_read) are CPU time of the process; perf_c_treedb is wall time. The page-by-page read rate is the mean of the FORWARD and BACKWARD passes of test_topic_pkey_integer_iterator5. perf_http and perf_micro are the drivers written for the 7.31.0 study, kept since. perf_timeranger2 of 7.32.0 has a new phase, rkey: its five figures have no side in 7.31.1 and are given as new figures. No hardware counters (perf_event_paranoid is 4 on this machine and no root). The rounds ran with the machine at rest, a load average of 0.4 to 1.
method.tag_run: The absolute figures of 7.32.0 are its side of the A/B run (318204992), measured on 2026-11-21. The binary sizes are those of the yunos of that worktree, built with the same .config (make, not installed).

story.title: Yuneta 7.32.0 against 7.31.1
story.lead: 7.32.0 closes a cycle of 28 lite releases (7.31.2 to 7.31.29, none with a study) and adds its own hardening: a regex that a peer sends to a store has a time bound, the filters of `list-agents` are bounded PCRE2 patterns, `help` takes linear time, and the BFF no longer gives one browser the session of another. Measured against 7.31.1, the last release with a study, before the tag: 61 of the 66 figures are inside their noise, three are faster and two are 2.2% to 2.4% slower. Every move was located by release, and none of them is new work per operation: the code on those paths is the code of 7.31.1, compiled and placed otherwise.

hero.text: the most that a regex sent by a peer can take from a store now. A live list of 3000 keys with a costly `rkey` is refused at 2.0 s, where 7.31.29 worked for 60.6 s, and an append with a cheap `rkey`, or none, costs what it cost.

tiles: Records read per second, page by page
treedb: update a node and save it
story.append_note: inside its noise against 7.31.1, in two runs of 10 rounds
story.ab_sub: Each benchmark built from the tree of each release (7.31.1 and 7.32.0), pinned to one CPU, the binaries run in rotation: 10 rounds. A change inside its whisker is noise. The eight figures outside their noise were measured again with 10 more rounds; the table at the end gives both runs in each reason.
story.prices_sub: Two figures are slower outside their noise, in both runs. Neither buys anything: the source of their paths is the source of 7.31.1, and each one moves with commits that do not touch it, so they are code generation and placement, located by release and by commit below. One price is paid on purpose and these benchmarks do not see it: on a follower, the check of the closed lists. Measured for the CHANGELOG against 7.31.29, 1000 appends read by a follower take 14.9 ms instead of 12.8 with 100 memory lists (+16%), 86.2 ms instead of 79.2 with 1000 (+9%), 48.8 ms instead of 44.2 with 8 disk feeds of 1000 lists (+10%), and 2329 ms instead of 2635 with 10000 lists (faster). It buys a follower whose callbacks can open and close lists without corrupting the batch.
prices: treedb: link or unlink two nodes
story.abs_sub: Absolute figures of the 7.32.0 build (318204992, its version commit), measured on 2026-11-21 on the laptop above, as its side of the A/B run: one process, pinned to one CPU. Mean of the 10 rounds.

new.title: New in 7.32.0: an rkey has a time bound
new.sub: An `rkey` is a regular expression (PCRE2) that selects the keys of a timeranger2 topic: a GUI that follows some devices sends one, and a peer with `read` permission can send any. In 7.31.29 a costly pattern held a single-thread yuno for seconds to minutes. 7.32.0 judges each key once, keeps the verdict, and gives each judgement a budget: a first search with 8 frames at each start position, then 2 ms of positions, and 2 s for the whole load of a list. The new `rkey` phase of `perf_timeranger2` measures both ends: what an ordinary append pays, and how a worst case ends. 7.31.1 has no such phase, so these are new figures, with no A/B.
new.note: Microseconds per operation, logarithmic scale: each grid step is ten times the one before. Mean of 10 runs of the 7.32.0 build. Grey: the run gave up or was refused at its budget, as designed, so its time is the bound, not a speed. The 7.31.29 figures in the table are those of the CHANGELOG, measured against 7.31.29 with this phase.

figures.meaning: A json of 2000 dicts of 3 keys.

figures.label: Append with a live list, no rkey
figures.meaning: One append over 100 keys with one keyless rt_mem list open, with no rkey: what a writer pays while a client follows the topic. 200 000 appends; every record reaches the list.

figures.label: Append with a live list, cheap rkey
figures.meaning: The same with the rkey `^0+1$`: one key of the 100 goes to the list. The verdict of each key is kept, so a key is judged once, not at each append.

figures.label: Append of a known key, costly rkey
figures.meaning: 200 appends over 20 keys of 20 digits with the rkey `(*NO_JIT)^(0+)+$`, which reaches the limit of one match on 19 of them. The verdict is kept, so only the first append of a key pays for it (11.5 ms an append in 7.31.29, measured for the CHANGELOG).

figures.label: First append of a new key, worst rkey
figures.meaning: The first append of 200 new keys of 255 bytes while a list with an unanchored rkey, costly at every position, is open: what a writer pays for a new key, once for each list. Every key is given up at its budget, a first search and then 2 ms of positions (158 ms a key in 7.31.29, measured for the CHANGELOG).
figures.gave_up: every key given up at its budget: the bound, not a speed

figures.label: Load of a live list, worst rkey
figures.short: Load of a list, worst rkey
figures.meaning: The load of a live list over 3000 keys of 36 bytes with that rkey. The 2 s budget of a load refuses it before any record is read (60.6 s in 7.31.29, measured for the CHANGELOG).
figures.gave_up: refused at its 2 s budget: the bound, not a speed
